concepts.name: Evolution of Poverty Line Methodology in India: From Caloric Norm to Consumption Basket
key_dimensions: Shift from caloric-norm-based approach (Alagh Committee, 1979) to MRP-based consumption expenditure approach
Why caloric norms were abandoned — limitations of food-only poverty lines in a diversifying economy
Role of NSSO household consumption expenditure surveys as the data backbone across all committees
UPSC trap: Distinguishing 'minimum caloric requirement' basis vs 'normative consumption basket' basis

concepts.name: Tendulkar Committee: Mandate, Composition and Context (2005–2009)
key_dimensions: Appointed by Planning Commission in 2005; report submitted in 2009 — why the timing matters (11th Plan context)
Suresh Tendulkar's specific brief: review Lakdawala methodology and recommend revisions
Committee acknowledged urban poverty line as anchor and derived rural line from it — reversal of earlier approach
UPSC trap: Tendulkar Committee ≠ Tendulkar-Sen Committee; no such joint committee exists

concepts.name: Tendulkar Poverty Line: Methodology and Basket Composition
key_dimensions: Used Mixed Reference Period (MRP) consumption expenditure data from NSSO instead of Uniform Reference Period (URP)
Poverty line defined by per capita per month expenditure: ₹816 (rural) and ₹1000 (urban) at 2011–12 prices
Basket included: food, education, health, clothing, footwear, and non-food items — not just food/calories
UPSC trap: Tendulkar line is NOT a food-only line; it includes non-food expenditures unlike earlier Lakdawala line

concepts.name: Tendulkar Poverty Estimates: Headcount Ratio and Absolute Numbers
key_dimensions: Poverty ratio: 37.2% (2004–05) revised downward to 21.9% (2011–12) — dramatic decline over 7 years
Absolute poor: ~270 million in 2011–12 vs ~407 million in 2004–05
Rural poverty (25.7%) vs Urban poverty (13.7%) in 2011–12 — rural-urban divergence
UPSC trap: These figures are based on 2011–12 NSSO 68th Round data — not Census data

concepts.name: Lakdawala vs Tendulkar Methodology: Key Differences and Implications
key_dimensions: Lakdawala anchored on caloric norms (2400 kcal rural, 2100 kcal urban); Tendulkar used MRP consumption basket
Lakdawala used state-specific price deflators; Tendulkar used a uniform national poverty line with state-level adjustments
Tendulkar gave higher poverty estimates than Lakdawala for the same year — acknowledged 'undercounting' by earlier method
UPSC trap: Tendulkar revision led to MORE poor being counted, not fewer — politically significant for welfare targeting

concepts.name: Mixed Reference Period (MRP) vs Uniform Reference Period (URP): Data Collection Distinction
key_dimensions: URP: All consumption items recalled over 30 days — used in Lakdawala; tends to underestimate consumption of low-frequency items
MRP: Low-frequency items (clothing, durables, health, education) recalled over 365 days; food over 30 days
Modified MRP (MMRP): Further refinements used by Rangarajan — 7-day recall for food items for precision
UPSC trap: Tendulkar used MRP; Rangarajan used MMRP — this methodological difference partly explains different poverty estimates

concepts.name: Rangarajan Committee: Mandate, Composition and Context (2012–2014)
key_dimensions: Constituted in 2012 after Supreme Court criticism of Tendulkar poverty line as 'too low and unrealistic'
Headed by C. Rangarajan, former RBI Governor and Chairman of Economic Advisory Council to PM
Report submitted in June 2014 — just after new government formation, making its adoption politically sensitive
UPSC trap: Rangarajan Committee was set up to REVIEW Tendulkar, not replace Planning Commission methodology wholesale

concepts.name: Rangarajan Poverty Line: Methodology and Basket Composition
key_dimensions: Separate and independent derivation of rural and urban poverty lines — not anchoring one on the other
Basket included: normative food expenditure (calories + protein + fat requirements) + essential non-food expenditure (education, health, clothing, transport)
Used Modified Mixed Reference Period (MMRP) data from NSSO 2011–12
Per capita per month: ₹972 (rural) and ₹1407 (urban) — significantly higher than Tendulkar thresholds

concepts.name: Rangarajan Poverty Estimates vs Tendulkar Estimates: The Divergence
key_dimensions: Rangarajan estimated 29.5% poverty (2011–12) vs Tendulkar's 21.9% for same year — ~7.5 percentage point gap
Absolute numbers: ~363 million poor (Rangarajan) vs ~270 million (Tendulkar) — 93 million more poor
Rural poverty: 30.9% (Rangarajan) vs 25.7% (Tendulkar); Urban: 26.4% vs 13.7% — urban gap is strikingly large
UPSC trap: Higher Rangarajan estimate does NOT mean poverty increased — it means the measurement is more inclusive/realistic

concepts.name: Caloric and Nutritional Norms in Rangarajan Methodology
key_dimensions: Rangarajan retained nutritional anchoring: 2155 kcal/day (rural) and 2090 kcal/day (urban) — different from Alagh's 2400/2100
Added protein norm: 48g/day (rural), 50g/day (urban) — a methodological innovation absent in Tendulkar
Fat norm also incorporated — reflecting diversification of nutritional understanding
UPSC trap: Rangarajan is NOT a pure caloric-norm method; it uses nutrition as one anchor within a broader basket approach

concepts.name: Absolute vs Relative Poverty: Conceptual Distinction and Indian Context
key_dimensions: Absolute poverty: Fixed minimum threshold (caloric/expenditure) — basis of all Indian official poverty lines
Relative poverty: Defined as percentage below median income — used in Europe/OECD countries
India's choice of absolute poverty line criticized as 'too low' — Rangarajan an attempt to make it less unrealistic
UPSC trap: India does NOT use relative poverty as official measure; MPI (multidimensional) is separate from income poverty line

concepts.name: Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) vs Income/Consumption Poverty Lines
key_dimensions: MPI (UNDP/Oxford): 10 indicators across Health, Education, Living Standards — not based on consumption expenditure
India's official poverty line (Tendulkar/Rangarajan): Purely consumption-expenditure based — monetary poverty
NITI Aayog adopted MPI framework for India: National MPI uses 12 indicators; latest report shows 415 million exited poverty (2005–21)
UPSC trap: MPI and official poverty line give different poverty counts — conflating them is a common error; they measure different things

concepts.name: Planning Commission's Role in Poverty Estimation and NITI Aayog Transition
key_dimensions: Planning Commission was the nodal body for poverty estimation using NSSO data until its dissolution in 2014
NITI Aayog replaced Planning Commission in 2015 — no direct successor body for official poverty line estimation
India has NOT officially adopted Rangarajan line — last official figures remain Tendulkar-based 2011–12 estimates
UPSC trap: Post-2014, India has NO updated official poverty headcount ratio — a significant policy vacuum

concepts.name: NSSO Household Consumer Expenditure Survey (HCES): Role and Controversies
key_dimensions: NSSO conducts HCES approximately every 5 years — 68th Round (2011–12) was last used for poverty estimation
2017–18 HCES results were suppressed/withheld by government citing data quality concerns — unprecedented controversy
2022–23 HCES released in 2024 — shows increase in consumption but not directly converted to poverty estimates yet
UPSC trap: Poverty line estimates and HCES are separate — HCES gives consumption data; poverty line threshold determines who is 'poor'

concepts.name: State-Level Poverty Variations and Spatial Heterogeneity
key_dimensions: Tendulkar methodology allows state-specific poverty lines using state-level price adjustments over national line
High-poverty states (Tendulkar 2011–12): Chhattisgarh (39.9%), Jharkhand (36.9%), Manipur (36.9%) vs low poverty: Kerala (7.1%), Himachal Pradesh (8.1%)
Rural-urban divergence within states complicates welfare targeting — BPL lists often not aligned with poverty line
UPSC trap: National poverty ratio is a WEIGHTED AVERAGE — state-level figures can differ dramatically from national figure

concepts.name: BPL Census and Its Disconnect from Poverty Line Estimates
key_dimensions: BPL Census (Socio-Economic Caste Census 2011 for rural; separate survey for urban) uses deprivation-based criteria, NOT consumption expenditure
Poverty line headcount ratio ≠ BPL list beneficiaries — this mismatch creates inclusion/exclusion errors in welfare targeting
Supreme Court in various cases (e.g., PUCL vs Union of India) criticized arbitrary BPL criteria
UPSC trap: Tendulkar/Rangarajan lines determine POVERTY RATIO; BPL lists determine WELFARE BENEFICIARIES — these are methodologically separate

concepts.name: Criticisms of Tendulkar Poverty Line: Political and Academic Contestation
key_dimensions: ₹816/month rural (2011–12) = ~₹27/day — criticized as insufficient to buy basic food in most states
Supreme Court (2011): Called the poverty line 'neither scientific nor realistic' in the context of food security
Arjun Sengupta Committee finding: 77% of Indians living on less than ₹20/day — far more than Tendulkar's poor
UPSC trap: ₹20/day figure (Sengupta) is NOT a poverty line — it is a consumption vulnerability threshold; do not conflate with official poverty line

concepts.name: Poverty Line and Food Security Linkage: NFSA 2013 Connection
key_dimensions: National Food Security Act 2013 covers 75% rural and 50% urban population — far exceeding any poverty line estimate
Parliament chose broader coverage than Tendulkar/Rangarajan poverty ratios to avoid exclusion errors
Subsidized food grain entitlement: 5 kg/person/month at ₹1–3/kg for Priority Households
UPSC trap: NFSA coverage is NOT derived from poverty line — it is a political/policy decision independent of Tendulkar or Rangarajan estimates

concepts.name: International Poverty Lines: World Bank $1.9/day vs Indian Official Lines
key_dimensions: World Bank extreme poverty line: $2.15/day (2022, updated from $1.90) at 2017 PPP — used for global comparisons
India's Tendulkar line roughly corresponds to $1.25/day (2005 PPP) — broadly aligned with earlier World Bank extreme poverty threshold
Rangarajan line closer to World Bank's $1.90/day threshold — making Indian estimates more internationally comparable
UPSC trap: PPP conversion makes direct Rupee-Dollar comparison misleading — poverty lines are not simply currency conversions

concepts.name: Poverty Measurement and Gender/Social Group Disaggregation
key_dimensions: Neither Tendulkar nor Rangarajan lines are disaggregated by gender — household-level consumption assumed equally distributed
Intra-household inequality (especially gender) is a blind spot of consumption-expenditure-based poverty lines
SC/ST poverty rates consistently higher: Tendulkar 2011–12 — SC poverty 29.4%, ST poverty 43.0% vs national 21.9%
UPSC trap: Official poverty line does NOT capture intra-household inequality or individual-level deprivation — a structural limitation
